overview: This event ties together fuel system, full-stop landings, and heavy-weight landing considerations in a way that should already make sense before you step. You should be ready to brief what changes the plan, what numbers matter, and where the usual errors start once the workload climbs.

items.text: Full-Stop Landings is judged by how well you enter it, stay ahead of the aircraft, and recover without needing cleanup coaching.

children.text: Know the entry airspeed, altitude, configuration, and cockpit setup before you start the maneuver.
Landing to a full stop with nose-high main gear touchdown, aerodynamic braking, and safe rollout.

items.text: Heavy-Weight Landing Considerations is judged by how well you enter it, stay ahead of the aircraft, and recover without needing cleanup coaching.

children.text: Know the entry airspeed, altitude, configuration, and cockpit setup before you start the maneuver.
Fly no less than on-speed AOA (amber donut)—cross-check with airspeed to avoid going slow.
Heavier aircraft are less responsive to pitch and power inputs.
Sink rates increase faster—anticipate and counteract with coordinated power and trim.
Flare should be more gradual and extended—aircraft will settle faster.
Increase approach turn speeds by 3–5 KIAS when above 700–800 lbs fuel.
The usual trap is missing the setup picture, then trying to salvage Heavy-Weight Landing Considerations late.

items.text: Treat this as a cumulative EP brief. The instructor can move quickly between recognition, memory items, and the branch logic that decides whether you continue, land, or eject.

children.text: Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground
Be able to state the recognition cue before you recite the steps.
Know the associated N/W/Cs, not just the memory items.
Have a clear answer for when the EP becomes a PEL, forced-landing, or ejection problem.

studyNotes.summary: Keep Fuel System and Full-Stop Landings organized early, then know the immediate actions, branch logic, and N/W/C details before you start improvising.
